content.title: About
content.content: Cheesecake, plain is a classic dessert made from cream cheese, eggs, sugar and a baked crust of biscuits or sponge cake. It has a smooth, creamy texture and a mild sweetness, without added fruits, chocolate or nuts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest cheesecake recipes date back to ancient Greece, where they used feta cheese and honey.
The modern American cheesecake originated in early 20th‑century New York, where cottage cheese was replaced by cream cheese.
Cheesecake can be made without baking; it sets in the refrigerator thanks to gelatin or heavy cream.
The most popular style is New York cheesecake, known for its dense yet airy consistency.
In Japan, a “no‑bake” version called “soufflé cheesecake” is lighter and more airy.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cream cheese provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Cheesecake supplies both dairy and animal protein, supporting tissue repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 from dairy supports the nervous system and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Probiotic content
items.content: Some cream cheeses contain live cultures that can benefit gut microbiota.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Cheesecake quickly replenishes energy due to its fat and carbohydrate content.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy may experience reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar increase calories and can affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Cream cheese contains saturated fats, so those with cardiovascular concerns should limit portions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cheesecake is calorie‑dense; overconsumption may lead to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cheesecake chilled, sliced into portions. It can be garnished with berries, fruit coulis, or a dusting of powdered sugar. For a lighter touch, pair with fresh fruit or a berry compote.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cheesecake refrigerated, covered with plastic wrap or in an airtight container, for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze it wrapped in foil and placed in a freezer bag for up to 2 months. Thaw in the refrigerator before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Coconut cookie is a sweet baked treat made with shredded coconut, flour, sugar and butter. It has a crisp edge and a fragrant, slightly buttery flavor with pronounced coconut notes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coconut cookies are often made without eggs, making them suitable for vegetarians.
The shredded coconut provides natural moisture and aroma, allowing the recipe to use less added fat.
In many countries the cookies are topped with toasted coconut flakes for extra crunch and flavor.
Coconut cookies can be gluten‑free when a gluten‑free flour blend is used.
Traditional recipes sometimes replace white sugar with honey or maple syrup.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Shredded coconut contains dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Coconut provides medium‑chain triglycerides that are quickly metabolized for energy.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Coconut supplies potassium, magnesium and iron, important for electrolyte balance and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Coconut contains phenolic compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Lauric acid in coconut has antimicrobial activity that may aid the immune system.

items.title: Coconut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to coconut, ranging from skin rashes to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Coconut cookies are calorie‑dense due to fats and sugars, so they should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Added sugar can be problematic for people with diabetes or those trying to lose weight.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Coconut fat is primarily saturated; intake should be limited for those with heart disease risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Coconut cookies make a convenient snack, pair well with tea or coffee, can be crumbled into yogurt, ice cream, or used as a base for dessert tarts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to maintain crispness and prevent fat rancidity.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑fat Graham crackers are dry biscuits made from whole‑grain wheat flour, sugar, vegetable oils and a pinch of salt. They have a crisp texture, a mildly sweet flavor, and contain about 30 % less fat than regular Graham crackers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Graham crackers were originally created in the United States in the late 19th century as a healthier bread alternative.
The name “Graham” comes from the Graham flour, a type of whole‑grain wheat flour.
Fat reduction is achieved by replacing part of the butter with lower‑calorie vegetable oils.
They are often used as a base for desserts such as cheesecakes and fruit tarts.
In the U.S. they are commonly served with cheese, fruit jam, or peanut butter.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat provides dietary fiber that supports normal digestive function.

items.title: Reduced fat content
items.content: Lower fat makes them more suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains thiamine, niacin and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from whole‑grain flour helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Crackers raise blood sugar slowly, which helps with steady energy release.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: The product contains gluten and may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Despite reduced fat, sugar is present, so individuals with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Salt is added for flavor; excessive intake may contribute to high blood pressure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Graham crackers can be enjoyed as a snack, spread with cream cheese, peanut butter or jam, used as a crunchy base for desserts, or incorporated into layered casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, refrigerate to maintain crispness and prevent mold growth.

venison-or-deer-noodles-and-vegetables-e.title: Venison with Noodles and Vegetables in Tomato Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Venison is a lean meat from deer, rich in protein and iron. Combined with whole‑grain noodles, a mix of vegetables (excluding carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens) and a tomato‑based sauce (ID 1463), it creates a balanced dish high in nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Venison is considered a more diet‑friendly meat than beef because of its low fat content.
Tomatoes used in the sauce are high in lycopene, an antioxidant that supports heart health.
Traditionally, venison is featured in Northern and Scandinavian cuisines.
Durum‑wheat noodles retain their texture during long cooking times.
Vegetables such as zucchini, bell pepper and mushrooms add flavor and vitamins without many calories.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Venison provides all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: A 100‑g serving of venison contains less than 5 g of fat, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: Deer meat supplies high levels of heme iron and zinc, important for immunity and energy.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Lycopene enhances antioxidant intake and may reduce the risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tomatoes and noodles provide vitamin B6 and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Allergy to game meat
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to venison.

items.title: Sodium in the sauce
items.content: Tomato sauces often contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Digestive load
items.content: High protein content can be heavy for those with kidney issues.

items.title: Possible parasites
items.content: Venison should be cooked thoroughly to eliminate any potential parasites.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut the venison into bite‑size pieces, quickly sear, then simmer with noodles, vegetables (zucchini, bell pepper, mushrooms) and tomato sauce until cooked through. Serve hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs such as parsley or dill.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh venison refrigerated at +2‑+4 °C for up to 2 days, frozen for up to 6 months. Store noodles and sauce in airtight containers in a cool, dry place. Leftover dish should be cooled and refrigerated, and consumed within 24 hours.
